questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to stay within Europe (more convenient, Erasmus Grant, language, and cultural reasons). Vienna is central in Europe so many travel opportunities to surrounding areas. I had never visited but heard great things about the city (all true!!). Affordable housing/living prices (compared to other destinations or major capitals in Europe).

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very pleased with my choice of destination - it is an ideal exchange city in my opinion.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: No major issues allthough the process can seem a bit extensive/long/complicated from home. Lots of formulas and administrative processes. But when arriving it seemed fine and easy enough. Wien Universität was also easy enough to communicate with (communicated with my coordinator at my department which was easy!). Great orientation sessions by the international office and ESN network in the beginning also with all info we needed to register adress, arrival date, course selection etc.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
The international office had several info meets/events that you could attend upon arrival with lots of info and you got your certificate of arrival. The ESN network held some events (more social than assistance, but still fine!). 
And my own department (anthropology) held a small welcome event for exchange students (nothing crazy or very informative - we weren't many people but still good to attend). 
There was also a formal welcome event by the uni itself! So all in all we were taken good care off i think.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I'd give it 4 or 5. I had found most info already online so didn't need that much assistance and i think the uni/ESN/department did a good job at giving assistance. Only negative part is just that it all seems very complicated sometimes - so much paperwork, and lots of things to take care of when leaving/arriving. But it all worked out and all students are in the same situation :)

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very easy for me. I made a profile on WG-gesucht (good app/website). I was pretty early (several months before arrival) so i just started checking out prices and opportunities and found a great place. I made a profile for requesting housing and i got a few messages from people requesting me as a flatmate so it seemed to be okay easy, but i was also quite early compared to others. I recommend going through WG-gesucht or HousingAnywhere.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Lots of opportunities for housing (only off campus!). Kind of same market as Copenhagen - many live in shared flats which you find on WG gesucht or HousingAnywhere or maybe in other groups. Theres also student dormitories, but i heard mixed experiences from this. Pricing for dorms is maybe a bit expensive compared to what you get then, so i still recommend a shared flat :) 
On the uni website theres some info for exchange student and lots of dorms that they recommend, so i was quite satisfied with the proces + possibilities of finding housing.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I got lucky and found something great, cheap, and central.
Its a bit cheaper than in CPH in general but i think many people pay too much even for Vienna prices because landlords charge more for international people that don't know the price range and can't complain about it. I paid 450 euros a month and lived almost in the centre but i know people that payed 500-700 and lived in worse locations and worse apartments than me. It's definitely possible to find something in good locations for 450-550 and be aware of bad landlords.....

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The issue is you have to make your own schedule so when you find courses you have to constantly check that they don't overlap on days/times. In seminars theres mandatory attendance so it was difficult to find enough courses that didn't overlap because some of them changed weekdays or wasn't regular (some were like once a month only). 
Also in my department all the courses were only 5 ects which meant i had to do 6 courses which was a lot and very hard to structure it all so i didn't have any overlaps.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Course lists are available quite late before the start of the semester. Then you just register for lots of courses generally (more ects than you need) and then test the courses in the first weeks before the deregistration deadline (a few weeks after semester start). A bit weird process when you don't know it but also cool to test the courses. Sometimes you'll be on the waiting list but many people will deregister and then you'll get the spot. 
You find course lists in the site u:find and register in u:space where you also then deregister the ones you don't want to do anyway.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
Info about this was giving at the orientation session/welcome event by the international office. Theres different types of courses (lectures, seminars) but i think it was simple enough once we got started and i got all the info about their system. 
I also got questions answered by my mobility coordinator of my department via mail so it was fine.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes i wanted and also the extra ones i had registered for and then deregistered later. I also took 2 MA courses to try it and also because it was so hard to find enough (30 ects) BA courses in english that wasn't on the same days/times....

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Spend some time on it in the beginning. When the course list becomes available look at all the ones you want and see if its possible, make a schedule, check they don't overlap too much. Register for too many courses, try them out, and then deregister some.
I made my Learning Agreement after the deregistration period was done and i knew the exact courses i was taking.

Also remember after arriving in Vienna to go register your address at the municipal district office (the uni/international office gives info on it also). Must be done in person with a signed document. And you also have to deregister once you leave.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Generally i found the level quite low. I had some courses which i liked but also some courses i did not enjoy at all.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Some courses were good and some were not good at all. Even one of my MA courses wasn't the best so i think in general the department of anthropology at CPH is just a bit better. More progressive, modern, better professors etc. So i didn't have the best academic experience but i also wasn't expecting it to be better than UCPH. I also didn't prioritize the academic aspect of my experience massively but i still did very good in most of my courses. 
The workload around exams though was huuge. Writing exams in 6 courses is so much work. I know most local students never take 30 ects because the workload with 6 courses becomes too much. This is very annoying since its the end of the exchange.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Lectures (VO, means Vorlesung) are just lectures with a written exam of some sort at the end which is 100 percent of the grade. 
Seminars (SE or PS) is with continous assesment so you get assesed for work in class, participation, presentations etc. plus a final paper. I had a mix of the two kinds which i recommend. All seminars would be too much work but all lectures would be too boring i think.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
PS BM2 New Critical Perspectives
SE BM7 Selected Topics in Political Anthropology
SE MM3 Sexual identities and/or orientations
SE MM3: Thinking with Things: Anthropological approaches to material culture
VO Introduction to Circumpolar North
VO New critical perspectives in social and cultural anthropology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I really liked the seminar in political anthropology. 
I did not like the lecture in New critical perspectives in social and cultural anthropology. There was maybe 100 people in it, it was unstructured, not a great professor, not a lot of substance or valuable content. The seminar of the same name was fine though. 
I think the course list changes very often, maybe every year/half year, so not sure these classes will be available for next fall semester

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
None really. Theres a small fee for the ESN network (like 25 euros maybe). 
I ate out more than in CPH so more cost in personal spending + trips, events etc. 
I booked trips with the ESN network like a ski trip which cost a bit but its worth it to get some experiences and meet some people.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Housing was cheaper than in CPH. Going out for food and drinks is way cheaper so its very nice to go out for drinks and food and many people, also students, do it more often.
Transportation is cheap! 75 euros for a semesterticket that lasts all semester and then you take all transport in Vienna.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I don't know a lot about these opportunities. 
The Erasmus student network (ESN) hosted many events especially in the beginning and some of these were nice to attend.
I joined two sports activities at the USI sports institute.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The USI sports institute is cool for joining cheap sports of very different kinds! Check it out, the list of sports is avaible just before semester start and sells out quickly. I joined a runningclub (ca 45 euros) and a pilates course (ca 50 euros) and they were both once a week all semester and i was very pleased with it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The USI sports courses. 
ESN events, also they host trips like ski weekend og sightseeing trips to other areas like Salzburg etc. 

I recommend: 
All the museums all over Vienna, walking around looking at the architecture, sitting in traditional viennese cafes drinking coffee and eating cake, going to bars (beer is okay cheap, like 4-5 euros), going to Naschmarkt (flea market every Saturday but many bars/restaurants/food stalls all days a week), go hiking in the mountains and go to Heuriger (wine taverns, only in warmer months), if it's a winter semester then attend a Wiener ball (january/february) (i went to TU ball), visit all the christmas markets (in December), go to Donau, go to Prater... the list goes on and on.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I went on a skitrip with ESN, a self organized ski trip to Kitzbühel, a day trip to Bratislava. I went hiking in the mountains/hills around Vienna (look up the Stadtwanderwegs, they are great hiking routes in the areas around Vienna and often easy to reach with public transport. My favorite area to hike in/visit was Nussberg/Kahlenberg in the late summer for good hikes, good views, fresh wine in the great outdoor wine taverns.)

Many went on weekend trips to Prague, Budapest, Salzburg, Graz or other sourrounding cities! Really recommend,

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. It's a lot like Danish people/Copenhageners. The stereotype is that Viennese people are rude - i did not find it to be true, or i just didn't find them any different than Copenhageners. A lot like Scandinavians they are a bit more introverted, don't talk to strangers etc., but i think that suits me well being Danish. Everybody was kind if you got to talking.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: You generally meet more erasmus people than local people. I met some in classes but mostly i met local people through my thursday running club - but if you want to make friends in these scenarios you have to be a little out there and talk to the locals yourself, say hi, chat, ask for contact info etc.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
I didn't speak fluent german so maybe that was sometimes more foreign for me but i quickly caught on and it was fine. It's not hard to lean the basics. 
No big cultural differences.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
I like that Vienna has a great cafe-culture - people sit in cafes/bars and drink coffee, beers, chat, and just hang out or read. It's cheaper so more accesible and affordable to students and creates a great atmosphere and lively vibe with all the outdoor cafes. 
I also appreciated the very cultural vibe of the city with a lot of history, museums, architecture, lots of great thinkers, music artists/composers, just lots of art/history/academic culture...

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. It's a great choice of host destination!! The summer/late-summer/spring is wonderful but the winter is also great actually (christmas markets made it great ;)) so both semesters are great choices. 
2. Try to see a bit of the country and nature. Go skiing in the alps, hiking in the Wienerwald, go to Prater, Donau, all the great nature of Austria. 
3. Austria is a little bit traditional still and a bit bureaucratic. Lots of paperwork still when it could be digital. They also use cash still!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Attend ESN events to meet exchange students. There are options both at the Universität Wien and the TU (technical uni), you can attend at both of them! I also made friends from TU.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
I met a lot of great people and eventually made a very good small regular friend group. People are very outgoing and friendly because everybody is looking to meet new people so make sure to attend som events in the beginning and make an effort to make friends, and then you'll get a great group to share the experience with.  
It was also a rewarding experience for me to spent a lot of time in my own company (going on hikes alone, eating out alone, going to a bar/cafe alone, going to museums alone) - it was a healthy and good experience for me.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: As i think everybody might experience, i did deal with some homesickness in the middle of the stay. It's hard to avoid i would say, so just accept it and let i pass slowly, let your friends know how you feel (they might feel the same!!), and i even booked a weekend trip back to CPH to see some friends (its cheap and a 1,5 h flight). It lasted on and off a few weeks for me, and overall i loved being there and my new friends, but it was also hard to get into a routine and you do spend more time alone while on exchange than i've been used to. All of it is healthy/normal and i learned a lot from this experience.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
